frames.narration: An order service has 3 use cases and 7 files. The use cases call the SQL client, the payment SDK and the mail client directly, so the rules depend on all three.
Product asks to switch the payment vendor. Place order and cancel order both call the SDK, so 3 files are edited, and 6 other behaviours (rules, database, mail) sit beside the change.
The team moves to ports and adapters: 10 files. The core now owns the interfaces and the adapters point inward. To run the rules, 0 infrastructure files are needed, against 3 before.
The same vendor switch now edits 2 files: the vendor adapter and the wiring in Main. Unrelated behaviour in the edited files: 0. The rules did not change.

The plausible shortcut: the payment port copies the vendor's method names and status codes. The use cases check those codes too. The vendor switch now edits 5 files (2 use cases, the port, the adapter, Main) with 3 unrelated behaviours beside it, worse than no ports.

The opposite extreme: every small thing behind a port and a mapper, 16 files. Switching the database or vendor still edits 2 files. But adding one field to an order edits 7: 4 of them only copy the field on.

Over four changes (database swap, vendor switch, shipping rule, new field) the files edited are: direct calls 12, ports and adapters 9, vendor-shaped ports 12, everything behind a port 13. Unrelated behaviour: 24, 2, 7 and 3. Tests to run again: 17, 18, 25 and 22.

So put the interface where the core can own it, in the core's terms, and add a port only where a swap, a second entry point or a fake of it is plausible. The structure pays for rare swaps and fast rule tests, and costs a little on every ordinary change.
